title: Protecting eyes from sunlight
keyIdea: The Sun is far brighter than any lamp: full sun can be about 100,000 lux, around 250 times as bright as a classroom. Looking straight at the Sun can burn the back of the eye and the damage can last for ever, so never look at it, not even with sunglasses, binoculars or a telescope, or on a cloudy day. Protect your eyes with a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses marked UV400 or CE, and shade, and watch an eclipse only as a picture through a pinhole viewer.
familyTip: On a sunny day, make a pinhole viewer: prick a small hole in a piece of card, stand with your back to the Sun and let the light fall on a second card. Move the second card further away and watch the Sun's picture grow. Check your family's sunglasses for a UV400 or CE mark together.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: judge safe and unsafe ways to look near the Sun, measure light in lux, protect a child's eyes, size a pinhole Sun picture, check a robot.

kid: The Sun is a star. It gives off much more light than any lamp. On a sunny day it can be about 250 times as bright as your classroom.

Never look straight at the Sun. Its light is so strong it can burn the back of your eye, and that can hurt your eyes for ever. Sunglasses do not make it safe. Binoculars make it worse, because they gather even more light.
You can protect your eyes outside. Wear a hat with a wide brim. Wear sunglasses with a UV400 or CE mark. Play in the shade when the Sun is high.
Sunlight can also bounce off snow and water into your eyes, and it gets through clouds. To watch an eclipse, use a pinhole viewer. Stand with your back to the Sun and look at its picture on a card.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. England's Year 3 science asks children to recognise that light from the Sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect their eyes. Key words: light source, the Sun, brightness, lux, damage, retina, sunglasses, UV (ultraviolet), shade, reflect.

Looking at the Sun can cause solar retinopathy: the light burns the retina, and the damage may be permanent. No ordinary sunglasses make direct viewing safe; only certified solar eclipse viewers or a pinhole projector do. For daily wear, sunglasses should carry a UV400, CE or BS EN ISO 12312-1 mark, and a wide brim and shade cut the light reaching the eyes. Fresh snow reflects up to 80% of UV, and thin cloud lets most of it through.

A common mistake is to think a cloudy day, a quick glance or sunglasses make it safe to look at the Sun. Children also think any dark glasses protect: dark lenses without a UV filter make the pupil open wider. Many think the Sun is just a big lamp; the light meter scene shows full sun at about 100,000 lux against about 400 lux indoors.

In the lab your child sorts six ways of looking near the Sun into safe and not safe, measures four places with a light meter, picks three things that protect a child's eyes, drags the screen of a pinhole viewer to make the Sun's picture 3, 6 and 9 mm wide, and checks a robot.

practice.prompt: A pinhole viewer makes a picture of the Sun about 1 mm wide for every 107 mm of distance. The screen is {=107*a} mm from the hole. About how many mm wide is the picture?
practice.hint: Each 107 mm of distance gives about 1 mm of picture. How many 107s are there?
practice.explain: {=107*a} ÷ 107 = {a}, so the Sun's picture is about {a} mm wide. Further away gives a bigger picture.

practice.prompt: A classroom is about 400 lux. A shady spot on a sunny day is {a} times as bright. How many lux is that?
practice.hint: Multiply 400 by how many times brighter it is.
practice.explain: 400 × {a} = {=400*a} lux. Even shade on a sunny day is much brighter than indoors.

practice.prompt: Is it safe to look at the Sun if you wear sunglasses?
choices: No, never look straight at the Sun
practice.hint: Sunglasses are for bright days, not for looking at the Sun.
practice.explain: Sunglasses do not block enough light to look at the Sun. It can still burn the back of your eye.

practice.prompt: Which helps protect your eyes on a sunny day?
choices: A hat with a wide brim
Dark toy glasses with no mark
practice.hint: Which one shades your eyes from the light above?
practice.explain: A wide brim shades your eyes. Binoculars gather more light, and toy glasses with no UV mark do not block the harmful light.

practice.prompt: Why should you wear sunglasses when playing in the snow?
choices: Snow bounces sunlight up into your eyes
practice.hint: Think about what bright white snow does to light.
practice.explain: Fresh snow bounces back most of the sunlight, so your eyes get light from above and below.

pool.prompt: A lamp-lit room is about 500 lux. A sunny spot outside measures {=500*a} lux. How many times as bright as the room is the sunny spot?
pool.hint: Divide the sunny spot's lux by 500.
pool.explain: {=500*a} ÷ 500 = {a}. The sunny spot is {a} times as bright as the room.

pool.prompt: Sam moved the screen of his pinhole viewer from {a} cm to {=2*a} cm away from the hole. How many times wider is the Sun's picture now?
pool.hint: The picture's width grows in step with the distance.
pool.explain: Twice as far away makes the picture twice as wide. The answer is 2.

choices: Glasses with coloured plastic and no mark
pool.hint: Look for a mark that says the glasses block ultraviolet light.
pool.explain: A UV400 or CE mark shows the glasses block harmful ultraviolet light. Dark lenses alone are not enough.

pool.prompt: It is a cloudy day. Is it safe to stare at the Sun?
choices: No, never stare at the Sun
Yes, clouds block all the light
pool.hint: Clouds move, and some light always gets through.
pool.explain: Clouds can move away in a moment, and harmful light gets through them. Never stare at the Sun.

pool.prompt: How can you safely watch an eclipse?
choices: Use a pinhole viewer with your back to the Sun
pool.hint: The safe way means no sunlight goes straight into your eyes.
pool.explain: A pinhole viewer shows a picture of the Sun on a card, so you never look at the Sun itself.

pool.prompt: What can happen if you look straight at the Sun?
choices: It can burn the back of your eye for ever
pool.hint: The Sun's light is extremely strong.
pool.explain: The Sun can burn the retina at the back of the eye, and that damage may never heal.

pool.prompt: Which is the brightest light source?
pool.hint: Which one lights up the whole sky?
pool.explain: The Sun is far brighter than any lamp or torch: full sun is hundreds of times brighter than a lit room.

pool.prompt: Where is a good place to play when the Sun is high in the sky?
choices: In the shade of a tree
On bright white snow without sunglasses
pool.hint: Find somewhere the direct sunlight is blocked.
pool.explain: Shade blocks the direct sunlight, so less light reaches your eyes.
